Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 107, verses 1–3:

﴿Have you seen the one who denies the Recompense?﴾ ﴿For that is the one who drives away the orphan,﴾ ﴿and does not urge the feeding of the needy.﴾

The interrogative is used here to express wonder at the state of those who deny the Recompense (al-jaza'), and at the evil conduct that their denial produced. The wonder is thus directed at their denial of the Din and at what branches from it: driving away the orphan and not urging the feeding of the poor. This wonder has been phrased in a captivating arrangement (nazm mashuq), because a question about seeing one to whom the relative clause (silat al-mawsul) applies sends the listener's mind in various directions to grasp the purpose of this question. The denial of the Din is widespread among them, so it would not be a source of wonder; the listener therefore awaits what follows it, which is His saying: ﴿For that is the one who drives away the orphan.﴾

The insertion of the demonstrative noun and the relative noun after the fa' adds to the suspense, so that the relative clause strikes the listener's hearing and takes firm hold of him.

The apparent original form of the speech would be: "Have you seen the one who denies the Din, who drives away the orphan and does not urge the feeding of the needy?"

The reference to the one who denies the Din with a demonstrative is to distinguish him in the most complete way, so that the listener may reflect upon him and his attribute, or to place him in the position of the manifest and clear, such that he is pointed to.

The fa' serves to coordinate the second attribute upon the first, to indicate that the combination of the two attributes causes the intended judgment of the speech. This is its function in the coordination of attributes when their subject is one, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By those who line up in ranks,﴾ [al-Saffat: 1] ﴿and those who drive away with a driving,﴾ [al-Saffat: 2] ﴿and those who recite the reminder,﴾ [al-Saffat: 3].

So the meaning of the verse is the coordination of the two attributes, driving away the orphan and not feeding the needy, upon the firm denial of the Din.

This indicates the repulsiveness of denying the resurrection, through what arises from its denial of blameworthy acts and of opposition to the truth, and of conflict with what wisdom requires of obligation. In this is a kinayah (allusion) warning the Muslims against approaching either of these two attributes, since they are attributes of those who do not believe in the Recompense.

The verbs in (yukadhdhibu, yaddu', and yahuddu) are in the present form to indicate the recurrence of that from him and its continuance.

This is a notice that faith in the resurrection and the Recompense is the true restraint which plants in the soul the roots of turning to righteous deeds, which become a disposition for it when it is raised upon them; so it grows pure and is drawn toward good without hardship, and without need for a command or for fear of one who inflicts punishments upon him. But when he is alone with himself and secure from watchers, he commits indecency and abominable deeds.

The seeing (al-ru'yah) is visual, and its verb extends to one object. The deniers of the Din are well known and their deeds are notorious, so their fame in this regard takes the place of a manifest matter that is seen.

Nafi' read the hamza that comes after the ra' in (ara'ayta) as an alif, with facilitation. The Egyptians narrated from Warsh from Nafi' its replacement by an alif, and this is what we recited in Tunisia. Likewise in the verb (ra'a), whenever an interrogative follows the hamza, this is to avoid pronouncing the two hamzas. The majority read it with full realization of the hamza.

al-Kisa'i read it by dropping the hamza after the ra' in every verb of this kind.

The relative noun and its relative clause are meant to denote the class of those who are characterized by this. Most of the exegetes have followed this view.

It was said: it was revealed concerning al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi. It was said: concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi. It was said: concerning 'Amr ibn 'A'idh al-Makhzumi. It was said: concerning Abu Sufyan ibn Harb before his Islam, because he used to slaughter a camel every week; once an orphan came to him and asked him for some of its meat, and he struck him with a staff. It was said: concerning Abu Jahl, who was guardian (wasiy) over an orphan; the orphan came to him naked asking him for some of his own property, and he pushed him away with a terrible push.

Those who held that the surah is Medinan said: it was revealed concerning a hypocrite whom they did not name. These are sayings some of which are attributed to some of the Tabi'un. Even if one of them were fixed upon a specific person, the cause of revelation would not restrict its ruling to what it was revealed about.

The meaning of (yaddu') is to push with violence and force. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿On the Day they will be pushed into the fire of Hell with a pushing.﴾ [al-Tur: 13].

Al-hadd: urging, which is that you demand from another a deed with emphasis.

Al-ta'am: the noun of feeding, a verbal noun (ism masdar) which is added to its object by a verbal (lafziyya) idafah. It is permissible that al-ta'am be meant as what is fed, as in His saying: ﴿Look at your food and your drink﴾ [al-Baqarah: 259]; then the idafah of ta'am to al-miskin is a ma'nawi idafah in the sense of the preposition li, that is: the food which is his right upon the rich. There would then be an omitted noun governed by (ʿala), its estimate being: upon giving the food of the needy.

The negation of urging is used as a metonymy for the negation of feeding, because one who is stingy in urging others to feed is even more stingy in feeding himself, as has preceded in His saying: ﴿And you do not urge one another to feed the needy﴾ [al-Fajr: 18] in Surat al-Fajr, and His saying: ﴿And does not urge the feeding of the needy﴾ [al-Haqqah: 34] in Surat al-Haqqah.

Al-miskin: the poor; it is applied to one of severe poverty. It has already been discussed at His saying: ﴿Charity is only for the poor and the needy﴾ [al-Tawbah: 60] in Surat al-Tawbah.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 107, verses 4–7:**

﴿So woe to those who pray,﴾ ﴿who are heedless of their prayer,﴾ ﴿who make a show [of their deeds],﴾ ﴿and withhold [simple] assistance.﴾

The placement of the *fa'* (so) clearly indicates that what follows is connected to what precedes it in the discourse, in the sense of consequence (*tafri'*), sequence (*tartib*) and causation (*tasabbub*).

[Page 567]

On the view that the whole surah is Meccan, it follows that the referent of "those who pray" is the same as the referent of "the one who denies the Recompense, who repulses the orphan and does not urge the feeding of the needy." Thus His saying "*lil-musallin*" (for those who pray) is a noun used in place of a pronoun (*izhar fi maqam al-idmar*), as if it had been said: "Woe to him for his heedlessness regarding prayer, for his showing off, and for withholding assistance." What prompted this is the increase in the enumeration of his blameworthy qualities through a flawless style that avoids a succession of six attributes. For such a succession does not avoid frequent repetition of similar items, and so it resembles the succession of genitive constructions (*idafat*), which is said to be detrimental to eloquence. Together with the insertion of "woe to him" in the middle, this signals that the woe arises from all those qualities of which he is deserving. This meaning is alluded to, obscurely, in the words of al-Kashshaf (Zamakhshari).

Accordingly, describing them as "those who pray" is then a mockery (*tahakkum*), and what is intended is its negation, i.e., those who do not pray, that is, who are not Muslims, as in His saying: ﴿They will say, "We were not of those who prayed, nor did we feed the needy."﴾ (al-Muddaththir 74:43). The indication of the mockery is the description ﴿who are heedless of their prayer﴾.

On the view that the surah is Medinan, or that this verse and what follows it are Medinan, the referent of "those who pray" who are heedless of their prayer is the hypocrites (*munafiqun*). This was transmitted by Ibn Wahb and Ashhab from Malik. In that case the *fa'* in His saying "So woe to those who pray" is part of this sentence, linking it to what precedes it, because God intended the connection of this discourse, part to part.

The plural form is used for this attribute because the referent of ﴿the one who denies the Recompense﴾ (al-Ma'un 107:1) is, according to the most apparent opinions, the category of deniers. If its referent is a specific individual according to one of the earlier opinions, the plural form is a way of generalizing (*tadhlil*) so that it includes him and others, since he is one of those characterized by abandoning prayer, by showing off, and by withholding assistance.

His saying ﴿who are heedless of their prayer﴾ is an attribute of "those who pray," restricting the applicability of the judgment to the described (*muqayyida li-hukm al-mawsuf*). For the woe is for the one who prays while being heedless of his prayer, not for the one who prays in general.

Thus His saying ﴿who are heedless of their prayer﴾ serves as a reinforcement (*tarshih*) of the mockery that occurs in applying the description "those who pray" to them.

"Heedless" (*sahun*) is construed with *'an* to indicate that they went beyond establishing their prayer and abandoned it, and this verse has no connection with the rulings on forgetfulness in prayer.

[Page 568]

And His saying ﴿who are heedless of their prayer﴾ may mean: those who perform prayer only for show, and when they are alone they abandon prayer.

It may also mean: those who pray without intention and sincerity, so that during prayer they are like one who is heedless of what he is doing. Then the application of "heedless" (*sahun*) is mockery, as He said: ﴿They show off to people and remember God only a little﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:142), concerning the hypocrites in Surah al-Nisa'.

"Showing off" (*yura'un*) means that they intend that people see them in a good state while they are otherwise, so that people speak well of them for qualities they do not possess. For this reason it is common to conjoin "reputation-seeking" (*sum'ah*) with showing off, saying "*riya'* and *sum'ah*." This verb occurs in speech in the *mufa'alah* form, and no simple form of it has been heard, because it necessarily involves repeated display.

"*Ma'un*" is applied to assistance with property, so the meaning is: they withhold their surplus, or they withhold charity to the poor. Charity was obligatory in the early period of Islam, without specification, before the legislation of *zakat*.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and Ibn Shihab said: "*al-ma'un*" is property in the language of Quraysh.

Ashhab transmitted from Malik: "*al-ma'un*" is *zakat*. The verse of the shepherd (*ra'i*) supports this:

"A people who, in Islam, have not withheld their *ma'un*, and have not neglected the *tahlil*."

For by *tahlil* he meant prayer, and so he combined it with *zakat*.

It is also applied to what is used in household work, such as vessels and implements for cooking, tying, digging and the like, which involve no loss to their owner in lending or giving them. And from 'A'isha: "*al-ma'un*" is water, fire and salt. This is a condemnation of them with the utmost stinginess, namely, withholding what does not diminish them.

The fronting of the subject (*musnad ilayh*) before the verbal predicate in His saying ﴿they show off﴾ serves to strengthen the judgment, that is, to affirm it.

As for the view that the surah is Medinan, or that these three verses are Medinan, the referent of "those who pray" is ﴿those who are heedless of their prayer,﴾ and the attributes following it refer to the hypocrites.

[Page 569]

Then the application of "those who pray" to them means "those who make a show of praying," and this is an application of the verb to its outward form, as in His saying: ﴿The hypocrites are wary lest a surah be sent down about them﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:64), that is, they show that they are wary of the sending down of a surah.

﴿And withhold [assistance]﴾, that is, charity or *zakat*. He said concerning the hypocrites: ﴿and they withhold their hands﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:67). When they became known by these traits, the implication of the *fa'* of consequence is that those who make a show of prayer while in their private lives abandoning it, are among those who deny the Recompense, who repulse the orphan and do not urge the feeding of the needy.

Hibat Allah ibn Salama related in *Kitab al-Nasikh wa al-Mansukh* (the book on abrogating and abrogated verses) that these three verses were revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul. That is, the plural form applied to him is used to mean one person, in the manner of His saying: ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 26:105), that is, the messenger sent to them.

The primary meaning of "*sahw*" (heedlessness) is forgetfulness of a matter whose knowledge has preceded. Here it is used metaphorically for turning away and abandoning deliberately, as a mocking metaphor (*isti'arah tahakkumiyyah*), like His saying: ﴿and you forget what you associate [with God]﴾ (al-An'am 6:41), that is, you turn away from them. Similar is the metaphorical use of "heedlessness" for turning away in His saying: ﴿because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them﴾ (al-A'raf 7:136) in Surah al-A'raf, and His saying: ﴿and those who are heedless of Our signs﴾ (Yunus 10:7) in Surah Yunus. The intent is not a threat over genuine forgetfulness regarding prayer, because the ruling on forgetting is lifted for this community, and this indicates that describing them as "those who pray" is mockery of them, that they do not pray.

Know that when God wishes to send down a part of the Qur'an appended to something before it, He makes the arrangement of the appended part suited to what is connected to it, so the *fa'* is for consequence. This is a subtle point that we have not previously had occasion to make clear, so you should attend to it in every passage known to have been revealed as an appendage to something revealed before it.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

**Surah al-Kawthar**

This surah is named "Surah al-Kawthar" in all the copies of the Qur'an we have seen and in all the exegeses as well. Al-Tirmidhi likewise titled it so in the Book of Tafsir in his *Jami'*. Al-Bukhari titled it in his *Sahih* as the surah of "*Inna a'taynaka al-Kawthar*" (Surah al-Kawthar 108:1). It was not counted by al-Suyuti in *al-Itqan* among the surahs that have only one name.

Sa'd Allah, known as Sa'di, in his gloss on the commentary of al-Baydawi, reported from al-Biqa'i that it is also called "Surah al-Nahr" (the surah of sacrifice). Is it Meccan or Medinan? The reports and opinions concerning whether it is Meccan or Medinan conflict strongly. It is Meccan according to the majority, and most exegetes limited themselves to this view. Al-Khafaji reported from the book *al-Nashr* that it said: "All those we know agree that it is Meccan." Al-Khafaji said: "There is room for doubt in this, given that there is disagreement about it."

From al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatada and 'Ikrima, it is Medinan. What supports them is what is in the *Sahih* of Muslim from Anas ibn Malik: "One day the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was among us, when he dozed off briefly, then raised his head and said: 'A surah has just been revealed to me,' and he recited, 'In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar. So pray to your Lord and sacrifice. Indeed, the one who hates you is the one cut off' (al-Kawthar 108:1–3). Then he said: 'Do you know what al-Kawthar is?' We said: 'God and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'It is a river which my Lord, Mighty and Majestic, promised me, upon which there is abundant good. It is a basin to which my community will come on the Day of Resurrection,'" and so on, the hadith. Anas embraced Islam at the beginning of the Hijra. If the word "*a'nifan*" ("just now") in the speech of the Prophet (ﷺ) is used in its apparent meaning, namely a recent time, then the surah was revealed shortly after that vision.

What is reported in the interpretation of His saying ﴿Indeed, the one who hates you is the one cut off﴾ (al-Kawthar 108:3) requires that the surah be Meccan, while the apparent interpretation of His saying "and sacrifice," that the sacrifice is at the Hajj or on the day of *al-Adha*, requires that the surah be Medinan. It also suggests that His saying ﴿Indeed, the one who hates you is the one cut off﴾

[Page 572]

is not a reply to the speech of al-'As ibn Wa'il, as we will explain.

The more evident view is that this surah is Medinan, and on this basis we will rely in explaining its verses.

Then the application of "heedless" (*sahun*) is mockery, as He said: ﴿They show off to people and remember God only a little﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:142), concerning the hypocrites in Surah al-Nisa'.

"Showing off" (*yura'un*) means that they intend that people see them in a good state while they are otherwise, so that people speak well of them for qualities they do not possess. For this reason it is common to conjoin "reputation-seeking" (*sum'ah*) with showing off, saying "*riya'* and *sum'ah*." This verb occurs in speech in the *mufa'alah* form, and no simple form of it has been heard, because it necessarily involves repeated display.

"*Ma'un*" is applied to assistance with property, so the meaning is: they withhold their surplus, or they withhold charity to the poor. Charity was obligatory in the early period of Islam, without specification, before the legislation of *zakat*.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and Ibn Shihab said: "*al-ma'un*" is property in the language of Quraysh.

Ashhab transmitted from Malik: "*al-ma'un*" is *zakat*. The verse of the shepherd (*ra'i*) supports this:

"A people who, in Islam, have not withheld their *ma'un*, and have not neglected the *tahlil*."

For by *tahlil* he meant prayer, and so he combined it with *zakat*.

It is also applied to what is used in household work, such as vessels and implements for cooking, tying, digging and the like, which involve no loss to their owner in lending or giving them. And from 'A'isha: "*al-ma'un*" is water, fire and salt. This is a condemnation of them with the utmost stinginess, namely, withholding what does not diminish them.

The fronting of the subject (*musnad ilayh*) before the verbal predicate in His saying ﴿they show off﴾ serves to strengthen the judgment, that is, to affirm it.

As for the view that the surah is Medinan, or that these three verses are Medinan, the referent of "those who pray" is ﴿those who are heedless of their prayer,﴾ and the attributes following it refer to the hypocrites.

[Page 569]

Then the application of "those who pray" to them means "those who make a show of praying," and this is an application of the verb to its outward form, as in His saying: ﴿The hypocrites are wary lest a surah be sent down about them﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:64), that is, they show that they are wary of the sending down of a surah.

﴿And withhold [assistance]﴾, that is, charity or *zakat*. He said concerning the hypocrites: ﴿and they withhold their hands﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:67). When they became known by these traits, the implication of the *fa'* of consequence is that those who make a show of prayer while in their private lives abandoning it, are among those who deny the Recompense, who repulse the orphan and do not urge the feeding of the needy.

Hibat Allah ibn Salama related in *Kitab al-Nasikh wa al-Mansukh* (the book on abrogating and abrogated verses) that these three verses were revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul. That is, the plural form applied to him is used to mean one person, in the manner of His saying: ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 26:105), that is, the messenger sent to them.

The primary meaning of "*sahw*" (heedlessness) is forgetfulness of a matter whose knowledge has preceded. Here it is used metaphorically for turning away and abandoning deliberately, as a mocking metaphor (*isti'arah tahakkumiyyah*), like His saying: ﴿and you forget what you associate [with God]﴾ (al-An'am 6:41), that is, you turn away from them. Similar is the metaphorical use of "heedlessness" for turning away in His saying: ﴿because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them﴾ (al-A'raf 7:136) in Surah al-A'raf, and His saying: ﴿and those who are heedless of Our signs﴾ (Yunus 10:7) in Surah Yunus. The intent is not a threat over genuine forgetfulness regarding prayer, because the ruling on forgetting is lifted for this community, and this indicates that describing them as "those who pray" is mockery of them, that they do not pray.

Know that when God wishes to send down a part of the Qur'an appended to something before it, He makes the arrangement of the appended part suited to what is connected to it, so the *fa'* is for consequence. This is a subtle point that we have not previously had occasion to make clear, so you should attend to it in every passage known to have been revealed as an appendage to something revealed before it.

[Page 570]

[Page 571]

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

**Surah al-Kawthar**

This surah is named "Surah al-Kawthar" in all the copies of the Qur'an we have seen and in all the exegeses as well. Al-Tirmidhi likewise titled it so in the Book of Tafsir in his *Jami'*. Al-Bukhari titled it in his *Sahih* as the surah of "*Inna a'taynaka al-Kawthar*" (Surah al-Kawthar 108:1). It was not counted by al-Suyuti in *al-Itqan* among the surahs that have only one name.

Sa'd Allah, known as Sa'di, in his gloss on the commentary of al-Baydawi, reported from al-Biqa'i that it is also called "Surah al-Nahr" (the surah of sacrifice). Is it Meccan or Medinan? The reports and opinions concerning whether it is Meccan or Medinan conflict strongly. It is Meccan according to the majority, and most exegetes limited themselves to this view. Al-Khafaji reported from the book *al-Nashr* that it said: "All those we know agree that it is Meccan." Al-Khafaji said: "There is room for doubt in this, given that there is disagreement about it."

From al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatada and 'Ikrima, it is Medinan. What supports them is what is in the *Sahih* of Muslim from Anas ibn Malik: "One day the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was among us, when he dozed off briefly, then raised his head and said: 'A surah has just been revealed to me,' and he recited, 'In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar. So pray to your Lord and sacrifice. Indeed, the one who hates you is the one cut off' (al-Kawthar 108:1–3). Then he said: 'Do you know what al-Kawthar is?' We said: 'God and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'It is a river which my Lord, Mighty and Majestic, promised me, upon which there is abundant good. It is a basin to which my community will come on the Day of Resurrection,'" and so on, the hadith. Anas embraced Islam at the beginning of the Hijra. If the word "*a'nifan*" ("just now") in the speech of the Prophet (ﷺ) is used in its apparent meaning, namely a recent time, then the surah was revealed shortly after that vision.

What is reported in the interpretation of His saying ﴿Indeed, the one who hates you is the one cut off﴾ (al-Kawthar 108:3) requires that the surah be Meccan, while the apparent interpretation of His saying "and sacrifice," that the sacrifice is at the Hajj or on the day of *al-Adha*, requires that the surah be Medinan. It also suggests that His saying ﴿Indeed, the one who hates you is the one cut off﴾

[Page 572]

is not a reply to the speech of al-'As ibn Wa'il, as we will explain.

The more evident view is that this surah is Medinan, and on this basis we will rely in explaining its verses.

On the view that it is Meccan, they counted it the fifteenth in the order of the revelation of surahs; it was revealed after Surah al-'Adiyat and before Surah al-Takathur. On the view that it is Medinan, it has been said that it was revealed at al-Hudaybiyah.

Its verse count is three, by consensus.

It is the shortest of the surahs of the Qur'an in number of words and number of letters. As for the number of verses, Surah al-'Asr and Surah al-Nasr are equal to it, but their words are more numerous.

\* \* \*

It includes the good tidings to the Prophet (ﷺ) that he was given abundant good in this world and the Hereafter, and a command that he thank God for this by devoting himself to worship.

And that this is the true perfection, not what the polytheists boast of over the Muslims in wealth and blessing, while they are the ones who have incurred the wrath of God, because they hated His Messenger; and the wrath of God is a cutting off for them when they are in the place of God's displeasure.

And the cutting off of a male offspring is not a true cutting off, because that has no effect on human perfection.
